article.markdown:
# A Gantt built for airline rotations worked as-is on a construction site

> **Build log series**: I hand my own design system `@gunjo/ui` ([Gunjo](https://gunjo.jp)) to an AI that has never seen it, and have it build real screens. This time I am expanding into construction. The brief: a **construction schedule screen for a site supervisor**. The screen combines schedule bars for each type of work, progress and work completed, the contractor in charge, milestones, weather, and site operations.

## Result: 4/5. The scheduling component crossed industries without modification

With only the public npm package and the gunjo.jp docs, the agent produced a construction schedule that passes `tsc` and works at both mobile and desktop widths.

**The `Gantt` scheduling component fit a construction schedule with almost no changes, even though it was not built for construction**. This `Gantt` was originally added to Gunjo for aircraft operating rotations and production-line resource planning. Its rows and time axis, the today marker, the interaction for selecting a bar and opening its details, and even its ARIA labels carried straight over to a schedule of construction work.

The existing components also fit naturally outside the schedule itself.

- **`Timeline`**: it handled milestones such as interim inspections, framing completion, and handover out of the box.
- **`Meter`**: its options for showing overall work completed against a target (`target` and the "higher is better" direction) mapped cleanly onto construction progress.
- **`DataTable`**: row clicks open details, and small meters can sit inside cells, so it covered both the list of work types and the detail view.
- **`StatGroup`**: it could correctly reverse the color meaning for a metric where an increase is bad, such as the number of delays.

Same components, different industry. Construction showed that the pattern holds.

## What was missing: dependency lines and progress inside the schedule bars

At the same time, two construction-specific requirements exposed clear gaps in Gunjo. Both are missing features in the scheduling component.

1. **There is no way to connect predecessor and successor work with lines.** I wanted to draw dependencies such as "the frame starts after the foundation is complete" as arrows between the schedule bars, but `Gantt` does not have that feature. This time I fell back to listing the preceding work as text in the detail panel. Dependencies are one of the most important parts of a construction schedule, so this is the largest gap.
2. **There is no way to fill a bar to show progress (work completed).** I wanted each bar to show how far that type of work had progressed, but this is not available as a standard feature either. This time I borrowed a mechanism intended for another purpose as a substitute.

I also had to hand-roll part of the color legend and the loading skeleton because the existing components did not cover either one. The hand-rolled portion was about 80 lines out of roughly 870 for the whole screen, so it was only a small part. I assembled most of the screen from existing components.

I follow the rule of three: a missing component gets built for real and added to Gunjo only after three separate screens have needed it independently. This is only the first appearance for the dependency lines and progress inside bars.

## Where the names got confusing

The scheduling components have similar names, which made the choice unclear. `ScheduleGrid` looks like the leading candidate from its name alone, but it is a timetable organized by period and day of the week, not a project schedule. `Gantt` was the right component. The names were not enough to decide, and the purpose became clear only after reading each description. The entry point for finding components by use case needs to be more prominent.

## Wrapping up

Construction is far removed from the foundational UI and finance screens I have covered with Gunjo before. Even so, I assembled the screen's foundation (the schedule, progress, work list and details, and milestones) from components built for other industries. I found only two construction-specific gaps: dependency lines and progress inside schedule bars. As I add more industries, I can see more clearly which components generalize and which gaps belong to a particular field.
